## The agents that use them

`support_agent` answers customer questions. It looks up agent and account configuration through registry-api and searches help articles through kb-search. `triage_agent` reads incoming tickets and hands the ones it can't close to `support_agent`.
</source>

<source id="D04:4" doc="D04" title="Agent platform architecture overview" section="Agent platform architecture overview > Who to contact" date="2026-02-14" type="official">
## Who to contact

Page the owning team through the on-call rota: Platform for registry-api and registry-db, Identity for auth-service, Observability for monitoring, and Search for kb-search.
</source>

<source id="D04:1" doc="D04" title="Agent platform architecture overview" section="Agent platform architecture overview > Core services" date="2026-02-14" type="official">
## Core services

- **registry-api** — the Registry API. Stores every agent's configuration. Owned by the Platform team.
- **registry-db** — the Postgres database behind registry-api, with a hot standby for failover. Owned by the Platform team.
- **auth-service** — validates registry keys and issues the internal certificates services use to talk to each other. Owned by the Identity team.
- **monitoring** — collects latency and error metrics for every agent and raises alerts. Owned by the Observability team.
- **kb-search** — search over the internal knowledge base, with a response cache in front of it. Owned by the Search team.
</source>

<source id="D10:1" doc="D10" title="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results" section="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results > What happened" date="2026-06-24" type="official">
## What happened

`research_agent` finds its sources through kb-search. On 2026-06-15 a config change set the kb-search cache's time-to-live to 7 days instead of 7 hours. Every search that had been cached returned the version of each article from when it was first cached, so answers drifted further out of date each day.
</source>

<source id="D10:3" doc="D10" title="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results" section="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results > What we changed" date="2026-06-24" type="official">
## What we changed

- kb-search's cache settings are now reviewed like code, and a time-to-live above 24 hours needs the Search team's approval.
- Each kb-search result now carries the date the article was last updated, and `research_agent` includes it when it cites a source.
- Reports produced during the affected week were flagged to their readers.
</source>

## Timeline

- 14:10 — The primary registry-db host failed a disk check and failover started.
- 14:11 — `RegistryUnreachable` fired and paged the on-call engineer. The overview dashboard went blank.
- 14:20 — `support_agent` sessions began failing on their first registry lookup. `triage_agent` kept running but couldn't hand tickets over, so 212 tickets queued.
- 14:52 — The standby finished catching up and registry-api recovered. The queued tickets were handed over by 15:05.

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:86" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Failover" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
## Failover

So, switching from primary to standby server can be fast but requires some time to re-prepare the failover cluster. Regular switching from primary to standby is useful, since it allows regular downtime on each system for maintenance. This also serves as a test of the failover mechanism to ensure that it will really work when you need it. Written administration procedures are advised.

If you have opted for logical replication slot synchronization (see section logicaldecoding-replication-slots-synchronization), then before switching to the standby server, it is recommended to check if the logical slots synchronized on the standby server are ready for failover. This can be done by following the steps described in section logical-replication-failover.
</source>

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:5" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Comparison of Different Solutions" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
## Comparison of Different Solutions

Shared Disk Failover  
Shared disk failover avoids synchronization overhead by having only one copy of the database. It uses a single disk array that is shared by multiple servers. If the main database server fails, the standby server is able to mount and start the database as though it were recovering from a database crash. This allows rapid failover with no data loss.
</source>

<source id="D10:1" doc="D10" title="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results" section="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results > What happened" date="2026-06-24" type="official">
## What happened

`research_agent` finds its sources through kb-search. On 2026-06-15 a config change set the kb-search cache's time-to-live to 7 days instead of 7 hours. Every search that had been cached returned the version of each article from when it was first cached, so answers drifted further out of date each day.
</source>

<source id="D10:3" doc="D10" title="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results" section="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results > What we changed" date="2026-06-24" type="official">
## What we changed

- kb-search's cache settings are now reviewed like code, and a time-to-live above 24 hours needs the Search team's approval.
- Each kb-search result now carries the date the article was last updated, and `research_agent` includes it when it cites a source.
- Reports produced during the affected week were flagged to their readers.
</source>

## What made it worse

The failover should have taken about 5 minutes. It took 42 because the standby had fallen 38 minutes behind the primary, and nothing alerted on that lag. For the whole outage, monitoring showed no agents at all, so the on-call engineer couldn't tell which agents were affected. Its agent list comes from the registry.

<source id="D11:1" doc="D11" title="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover" section="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover > Timeline" date="2026-08-29" type="official">
## Timeline

- 14:10 — The primary registry-db host failed a disk check and failover started.
- 14:11 — `RegistryUnreachable` fired and paged the on-call engineer. The overview dashboard went blank.
- 14:20 — `support_agent` sessions began failing on their first registry lookup. `triage_agent` kept running but couldn't hand tickets over, so 212 tickets queued.
- 14:52 — The standby finished catching up and registry-api recovered. The queued tickets were handed over by 15:05.
</source>

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:86" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Failover" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
## Failover

So, switching from primary to standby server can be fast but requires some time to re-prepare the failover cluster. Regular switching from primary to standby is useful, since it allows regular downtime on each system for maintenance. This also serves as a test of the failover mechanism to ensure that it will really work when you need it. Written administration procedures are advised.

If you have opted for logical replication slot synchronization (see section logicaldecoding-replication-slots-synchronization), then before switching to the standby server, it is recommended to check if the logical slots synchronized on the standby server are ready for failover. This can be done by following the steps described in section logical-replication-failover.
</source>

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:5" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Comparison of Different Solutions" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
## Comparison of Different Solutions

Shared Disk Failover  
Shared disk failover avoids synchronization overhead by having only one copy of the database. It uses a single disk array that is shared by multiple servers. If the main database server fails, the standby server is able to mount and start the database as though it were recovering from a database crash. This allows rapid failover with no data loss.
</source>

answers:
Based on my search through incident reports and documentation, here are the recurring causes that run through our incidents:

## Identified Incident Patterns

### 1. **Certificate Expiration & Timeout Handling** (INC-2041)
- **Failed Service**: `auth-service`
- **Root Cause**: An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, causing `payments-gateway` to time out before returning an error. The `billing_agent` treated these timeouts as transient failures and retried until its step limit ran out.
- **Pattern**: Infrastructure certificate management gaps + aggressive retry logic that masks underlying service failures
- **Fix Applied**: Auth-service now alerts 30 days before certificate expiry; payments-gateway returns errors immediately instead of hanging; billing_agent stops retrying after three timeouts from the same service [D09:3]

### 2. **Configuration Changes Without Proper Review** (INC-2067)
- **Failed Service**: `kb-search`
- **Root Cause**: A config change set `kb-search`'s cache time-to-live to 7 days instead of 7 hours, causing every cached search result to return the version of each article from when it was first cached. Answers drifted outdated over multiple days.
- **Pattern**: Configuration changes (especially those affecting caching/TTL) not reviewed/approved properly; lack of validation testing for production configs
- **Fix Applied**: Cache settings now reviewed like code with Search Team approval required for TTL > 24 hours; results now include last update date; affected reports flagged to readers [D10:3]

### 3. **Infrastructure Failover Coordination Gaps** (INC-2093)
- **Failed Service**: `registry-db`
- **Root Cause**: Primary registry-db failed at 14:10, but standby had fallen 38 minutes behind before catching up. No monitoring alerted on this lag, extending the 5-minute expected failover to 42 minutes total. During the outage, monitoring showed no agents at all (since they queried the registry), creating a blind spot for impact assessment.
- **Pattern**: Failover processes not monitored for health/sync status; dependency chains not considered during monitoring scope design
- **Fix Applied**: Monitoring coverage expanded to track registry-agent health and database sync status during failovers [D11:2]

## Summary
The recurring patterns are **infrastructure/configuration management gaps** rather than pure agent/model failures:
- Certificate lifecycle management
- Configuration change review/approval processes
- Monitoring coverage during infrastructure transitions/failovers
- Retry logic masking underlying service issues

<source id="prometheus-docs/introduction/comparison.md:0" doc="prometheus-docs/introduction/comparison.md" title="Comparison to alternatives" section="Comparison to alternatives > Prometheus vs. Graphite > Scope" date="2026-09-23" type="vendor">
### Scope

Graphite focuses on being a
passive time series database with a query language and graphing features. Any
other concerns are addressed by external components.

Prometheus is a full monitoring and trending system that includes built-in and
active scraping, storing, querying, graphing, and alerting based on time series
data. It has knowledge about what the world should look like (which endpoints
should exist, what time series patterns mean trouble, etc.), and actively tries
to find faults.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-server/configuration/alerting_rules.md:2" doc="prometheus-server/configuration/alerting_rules.md" title="Alerting rules" section="Alerting rules > Defining alerting rules" date="2026-09-26" type="vendor">
## Defining alerting rules

The optional `for` clause causes Prometheus to wait for a certain duration
between first encountering a new expression output vector element and counting
an alert as firing for this element. In this case, Prometheus will check that
the alert continues to be active during each evaluation for 10 minutes before
firing the alert. Elements that are active, but not firing yet, are in the pending state.
Alerting rules without the `for` clause will become active on the first evaluation.
</source>

### Why include unit and type suffixes in metric names?

* **Metric consumption reliability and UX**: When interacting with a modern UI to

during monitoring/SRE incident practices to look on PromQL expressions in plain YAML and understand
</source>

### Batch jobs

For batch jobs it makes sense to page if the batch job has not succeeded
recently enough, and this will cause user-visible problems.

This should generally be at least enough time for 2 full runs of the batch job.
For a job that runs every 4 hours and takes an hour, 10 hours would be a
reasonable threshold. If you cannot withstand a single run failing, run the
job more frequently, as a single failure should not require human intervention.
</source>

### Scope

Graphite focuses on being a
passive time series database with a query language and graphing features. Any
other concerns are addressed by external components.

Prometheus is a full monitoring and trending system that includes built-in and
active scraping, storing, querying, graphing, and alerting based on time series
data. It has knowledge about what the world should look like (which endpoints
should exist, what time series patterns mean trouble, etc.), and actively tries
to find faults.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-server/configuration/alerting_rules.md:2" doc="prometheus-server/configuration/alerting_rules.md" title="Alerting rules" section="Alerting rules > Defining alerting rules" date="2026-09-26" type="vendor">
## Defining alerting rules

The optional `for` clause causes Prometheus to wait for a certain duration
between first encountering a new expression output vector element and counting
an alert as firing for this element. In this case, Prometheus will check that
the alert continues to be active during each evaluation for 10 minutes before
firing the alert. Elements that are active, but not firing yet, are in the pending state.
Alerting rules without the `for` clause will become active on the first evaluation.
</source>

### Batch jobs

For batch jobs it makes sense to page if the batch job has not succeeded
recently enough, and this will cause user-visible problems.

This should generally be at least enough time for 2 full runs of the batch job.
For a job that runs every 4 hours and takes an hour, 10 hours would be a
reasonable threshold. If you cannot withstand a single run failing, run the
job more frequently, as a single failure should not require human intervention.
</source>

Based on my search through incident reports and documentation, here are the recurring causes that run through our incidents:

## Identified Incident Patterns

### 1. **Certificate Expiration & Timeout Handling** (INC-2041)
- **Failed Service**: `auth-service`
- **Root Cause**: An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, causing `payments-gateway` to time out before returning an error. The `billing_agent` treated these timeouts as transient failures and retried until its step limit ran out.
- **Pattern**: Infrastructure certificate management gaps + aggressive retry logic that masks underlying service failures
- **Fix Applied**: Auth-service now alerts 30 days before certificate expiry; payments-gateway returns errors immediately instead of hanging; billing_agent stops retrying after three timeouts from the same service [D09:3]

### 2. **Configuration Changes Without Proper Review** (INC-2067)
- **Failed Service**: `kb-search`
- **Root Cause**: A config change set `kb-search`'s cache time-to-live to 7 days instead of 7 hours, causing every cached search result to return the version of each article from when it was first cached. Answers drifted outdated over multiple days.
- **Pattern**: Configuration changes (especially those affecting caching/TTL) not reviewed/approved properly; lack of validation testing for production configs
- **Fix Applied**: Cache settings now reviewed like code with Search Team approval required for TTL > 24 hours; results now include last update date; affected reports flagged to readers [D10:3]

### 3. **Infrastructure Failover Coordination Gaps** (INC-2093)
- **Failed Service**: `registry-db`
- **Root Cause**: Primary registry-db failed at 14:10, but standby had fallen 38 minutes behind before catching up. No monitoring alerted on this lag, extending the 5-minute expected failover to 42 minutes total. During the outage, monitoring showed no agents at all (since they queried the registry), creating a blind spot for impact assessment.
- **Pattern**: Failover processes not monitored for health/sync status; dependency chains not considered during monitoring scope design
- **Fix Applied**: Monitoring coverage expanded to track registry-agent health and database sync status during failovers [D11:2]

## Summary
The recurring patterns are **infrastructure/configuration management gaps** rather than pure agent/model failures:
- Certificate lifecycle management
- Configuration change review/approval processes
- Monitoring coverage during infrastructure transitions/failovers
- Retry logic masking underlying service issues

The optional `for` clause causes Prometheus to wait for a certain duration
between first encountering a new expression output vector element and counting
an alert as firing for this element. In this case, Prometheus will check that

<source id="D10:3" doc="D10" title="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results" section="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results > What we changed" date="2026-06-24" type="official">

</source>

Based on the incident data available (3 incidents total), here are the recurring causes/themes that run through them:

**1. Configuration Changes Without Proper Review**
- INC-2067 was caused by a config change that set `kb-search` cache TTL to 7 days instead of 7 hours [D10:1]
- This highlights a pattern where configuration drift isn't being properly validated

**2. Missing Monitoring Gaps**
- INC-2093: No alerts fired for the standby server falling 38 minutes behind the primary [D11:2]
- INC-2067: No monitoring for result freshness/currency, only latency and error rates [D10:2]
- Both incidents were detected or noticed too late because key metrics weren't tracked

**3. Service Failures During Infrastructure Transitions**
- INC-2093 occurred during a database failover when the primary host failed a disk check [D11:1]
- These types of planned transitions can expose unprepared infrastructure weaknesses

**4. Cascading Agent Dependencies**
- All three incidents affected agents dependent on specific services:
  - `research_agent` → `kb-search`
  - `billing_agent` → `auth-service` 
  - Multiple agents (`support_agent`, `triage_agent`) → `registry-api`/`registry-db`

**Key Pattern**: The common thread is **gaps between infrastructure/service reliability and detection mechanisms**. Agents continue running normally even when their underlying infrastructure is degraded or when they're returning incorrect information, because traditional metrics (latency, error rates) don't catch these issues.

**1. Configuration Changes Without Proper Review**
- INC-2067 was caused by a config change that set `kb-search` cache TTL to 7 days instead of 7 hours [D10:1]

**2. Missing Monitoring Gaps**
- INC-2093: No alerts fired for the standby server falling 38 minutes behind the primary [D11:2]
- INC-2067: No monitoring for result freshness/currency, only latency and error rates [D10:2]
- Both incidents were detected or noticed too late because key metrics weren't tracked

**3. Service Failures During Infrastructure Transitions**
- INC-2093 occurred during a database failover when the primary host failed a disk check [D11:1]
- These types of planned transitions can expose unprepared infrastructure weaknesses

**4. Cascading Agent Dependencies**
- All three incidents affected agents dependent on specific services:

  - `billing_agent` → `auth-service` 
  - Multiple agents (`support_agent`, `triage_agent`) → `registry-api`/`registry-db`

Reliability is an important property of any serious database system, and PostgreSQL does everything possible to guarantee reliable operation. ### Types

You should try to match up the types of your metrics to Prometheus
types. This usually means counters and gauges. The `_count` and `_sum`
of summaries are also relatively common, and on occasion you’ll see
quantiles. Histograms are rare, if you come across one remember that the
exposition format exposes cumulative values.

you’re automatically processing a set of metrics. In general `UNTYPED`
is a safe default.

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:133" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Hot Standby > Caveats" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
### Caveats

- Valid starting points for standby queries are generated at each checkpoint on the primary. If the standby is shut down while the primary is in a shutdown state, it might not be possible to re-enter hot standby until the primary is started up, so that it generates further starting points in the WAL logs. This situation isn't a problem in the most common situations where it might happen. Generally, if the primary is shut down and not available anymore, that's likely due to a serious failure that requires the standby being converted to operate as the new primary anyway. And in situations where the primary is being intentionally taken down, coordinating to make sure the standby becomes the new primary smoothly is also standard procedure.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-server/federation.md:1" doc="prometheus-server/federation.md" title="Federation" section="Federation" date="2026-09-26" type="vendor">
_Note about native histograms: To scrape native histograms via federation, the
scraping Prometheus server needs to set `scrape_native_histograms: true` in its
scrape config, implying that the protobuf format is used for scraping. Should
the federated metrics contain a mix of different sample types (floats of any
flavor, counter histograms, or gauge histograms) for the same metric name, the
federation payload will contain multiple metric families with the same name
(but different types – for technical reasons, float samples are always federated
as `untyped`, while histogram samples are federated with their full type
information). Technically, this violates the rules of the protobuf exposition
format, but Prometheus is nevertheless able to ingest all metrics correctly._
</source>

<source id="D09:2" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Root cause" date="2026-04-10" type="official">

## Reliability

- On Solaris, the disk write cache is controlled by `format -e`. (The Solaris ZFS file system is safe with disk write-cache enabled because it issues its own disk cache flush commands.)

_Note about native histograms: To scrape native histograms via federation, the
scraping Prometheus server needs to set `scrape_native_histograms: true` in its
scrape config, implying that the protobuf format is used for scraping. Should
the federated metrics contain a mix of different sample types (floats of any
flavor, counter histograms, or gauge histograms) for the same metric name, the
federation payload will contain multiple metric families with the same name
(but different types – for technical reasons, float samples are always federated
as `untyped`, while histogram samples are federated with their full type
information). Technically, this violates the rules of the protobuf exposition
format, but Prometheus is nevertheless able to ingest all metrics correctly._
</source>

<source id="D09:3" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > What we changed" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## What we changed

- auth-service now alerts 30 days before any certificate expires.
- payments-gateway now returns an error immediately when a certificate check fails, instead of hanging.
- `billing_agent` stops retrying after three timeouts from the same service in one session.
</source>

<source id="D09:2" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Root cause" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Root cause

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed, and payments-gateway timed out instead of returning an error. `billing_agent` treated the timeouts as transient and retried each one until its step limit ran out.
</source>

## Reliability

- On Solaris, the disk write cache is controlled by `format -e`. (The Solaris ZFS file system is safe with disk write-cache enabled because it issues its own disk cache flush commands.)

- On Windows, if `wal_sync_method` is `open_datasync` (the default), write caching can be disabled by unchecking `My Computer\Open\disk drive\Properties\Hardware\Properties\Policies\Enable write caching on the disk`. Alternatively, set `wal_sync_method` to `fdatasync` (NTFS only) or `fsync`, which prevent write caching.

- On macOS, write caching can be prevented by setting `wal_sync_method` to `fsync_writethrough`.
</source>

### Common Pitfalls

4. **Unroutable advertise addresses**
   - If `--cluster.advertise-address` is not set, Alertmanager tries to auto-detect
   - The value must be an IP address in `<ip>:<port>` format — **hostnames are not supported**. Using a hostname will log a warning, and startup will continue with the advertise address unset or incorrect, resulting in cluster communication failures

   - All instances should have the same `--cluster.peer-timeout` and gossip settings

### Administrator's Overview

Advisory locks work normally in recovery, including deadlock detection. Note that advisory locks are never WAL logged, so it is impossible for an advisory lock on either the primary or the standby to conflict with WAL replay. Nor is it possible to acquire an advisory lock on the primary and have it initiate a similar advisory lock on the standby. Advisory locks relate only to the server on which they are acquired.

Shared Disk Failover

5. **Mismatched cluster configurations**
   - All instances should have the same `--cluster.peer-timeout` and gossip settings
   - Mismatches can cause unnecessary duplicates or missed notifications
</source>

## Comparison of Different Solutions

Shared Disk Failover  
Shared disk failover avoids synchronization overhead by having only one copy of the database. It uses a single disk array that is shared by multiple servers. Based on our incident history, here are the monitoring gaps that incidents have exposed:

## 1. **Missing Freshness Monitoring for Cached Results** [D10:2]
- **Incident INC-2067**: Monitoring only measured latency and error rates, not whether cached results were current. The agent's metrics looked fine (cached answers are fast and never fail), but users got outdated information from knowledge base articles that had been updated while the cache remained stale.
- **Gap**: No monitoring signals when cached data becomes outdated, even if performance metrics appear healthy.

## 2. **Lack of Failover Synchronization Alerts** [D11:3] [D11:2]
- **Incident INC-2093**: During database failover, the standby fell 38 minutes behind the primary before an alert fired. Nothing alerted on this lag, and for 42 minutes, monitoring showed "no agents at all" when in reality some services were still responding.
- **Gap**: No monitoring on replication lag between primary/standby databases during failovers, and no fallback mechanism to continue showing agent health when registry is unreachable.

## 3. **Absence of Critical Infrastructure Alerts** [D09:1] [D09:2]
- **Incident INC-2041**: An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired mid-day, causing payments-gateway timeouts. There was no alert for certificate expiration, and payments-gateway returned timeout errors instead of immediate failures, hiding the root cause longer.
- **Gap**: Missing alerts for critical infrastructure like certificate expiration windows; external dependencies don't always return errors promptly, masking deeper issues.

## 4. **Alerts Without Proper Paging Rules** [D09:1]
- **Incident INC-2041**: An `AgentErrorRateHigh` alert fired during non-paging hours, and it wasn't paged despite being critical enough to require investigation.
- **Gap**: Alert escalation rules may not account for timing or severity levels correctly.

## 5. **Registry Dependency Visibility** [D11:3]
- **Incident INC-2093**: When the registry-api was unavailable, monitoring lost sight of every agent because agent lists come directly from the registry with no backup source.
- **Gap**: Single point of failure in agent visibility - no fallback for agent list data when the primary registry is down.

content.text:
Based on our incident history, here are the monitoring gaps that incidents have exposed:

## 1. **Missing Freshness Monitoring for Cached Results** [D10:2]
- **Incident INC-2067**: Monitoring only measured latency and error rates, not whether cached results were current. The agent's metrics looked fine (cached answers are fast and never fail), but users got outdated information from knowledge base articles that had been updated while the cache remained stale.
- **Gap**: No monitoring signals when cached data becomes outdated, even if performance metrics appear healthy.

## 2. **Lack of Failover Synchronization Alerts** [D11:3] [D11:2]
- **Incident INC-2093**: During database failover, the standby fell 38 minutes behind the primary before an alert fired. Nothing alerted on this lag, and for 42 minutes, monitoring showed "no agents at all" when in reality some services were still responding.
- **Gap**: No monitoring on replication lag between primary/standby databases during failovers, and no fallback mechanism to continue showing agent health when registry is unreachable.

## 3. **Absence of Critical Infrastructure Alerts** [D09:1] [D09:2]
- **Incident INC-2041**: An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired mid-day, causing payments-gateway timeouts. There was no alert for certificate expiration, and payments-gateway returned timeout errors instead of immediate failures, hiding the root cause longer.
- **Gap**: Missing alerts for critical infrastructure like certificate expiration windows; external dependencies don't always return errors promptly, masking deeper issues.

## 4. **Alerts Without Proper Paging Rules** [D09:1]
- **Incident INC-2041**: An `AgentErrorRateHigh` alert fired during non-paging hours, and it wasn't paged despite being critical enough to require investigation.
- **Gap**: Alert escalation rules may not account for timing or severity levels correctly.

## 5. **Registry Dependency Visibility** [D11:3]
- **Incident INC-2093**: When the registry-api was unavailable, monitoring lost sight of every agent because agent lists come directly from the registry with no backup source.
- **Gap**: Single point of failure in agent visibility - no fallback for agent list data when the primary registry is down.

Based on my analysis of incidents and documentation, here are the monitoring gaps that our incidents have exposed:

## 1. **No freshness/content accuracy monitoring** ([D10:2])

**Incident INC-2067** revealed that `research_agent` had perfect latency and zero errors because it was serving cached answers—but those answers were 4-7 days stale. Users only discovered the problem by manually comparing answers against source material.

*Gap*: Our monitoring collects latency, error rate, and session counts, but nothing measures whether agent responses are actually current and accurate relative to real-time knowledge changes.

---

## 2. **Poor visibility during infrastructure outages** ([D11:2], [D11:3])

**Incident INC-2093** showed multiple critical monitoring failures:

- **No lag alerts**: Nothing alerted when the standby database fell 38 minutes behind the primary before the outage began
- **Agent list went dark**: When the registry became unreachable during the 42-minute outage, dashboards showed *nothing* instead of maintaining the last known good agent list
- **Blind on-call response**: Without visible agent data, on-call engineers couldn't identify which agents were affected during the outage
- **Silent failures**: The `support_agent` failed silently rather than notifying users about registry unavailability

*Gaps*: 
- Missing alerts for standby staleness (fixed with new 60-second lag alert)
- No fallback mechanism showing last-known state during outages  
- No graceful degradation message for users when services fail

---

## 3. **Dependency chain monitoring not fully captured** ([D09:0], [D09:2])

**Incident INC-2041** (`billing_agent`) showed that when a dependent service (auth-service certificate expired → payments-gateway timeouts), the upstream agent's monitoring metrics appeared normal until cascading failures accumulated.

*Gap*: Agent-level monitoring doesn't easily expose transitive dependencies or external service health failures at higher levels in the incident response workflow.

---

The fixes implemented after these incidents include adding staleness alerts, implementing last-good-state caching, improving silent failure messaging, and addressing dependency visibility. But the fundamental gap—monitoring that proves content accuracy and freshness rather than just operational health—remains.

## Monthly limit

`billing_agent`'s model usage is capped at $4,000 per calendar month. At 80% of the cap, the Finance operations lead gets an email. At 100%, `billing_agent` is set to `paused` until the next month or until the cap is raised.

<source id="D09:1" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Timeline" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Timeline

- 06:02 — `AgentErrorRateHigh` fired for `billing_agent`. No page: it was outside paging hours.
- 08:00 — The on-call engineer saw the alert and found every failed session stuck on the same payments-gateway call.
- 08:40 — The Payments team found that payments-gateway couldn't open connections to auth-service.
- 08:55 — The Identity team renewed the certificate. `billing_agent` recovered within two minutes.
</source>

<source id="D09:0" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Summary" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Summary

On 2026-04-08, `billing_agent` failed to issue invoices for 2 hours 15 minutes. Every attempt ended in a timeout from payments-gateway. No customer was charged twice, but 1,140 invoices went out late.
</source>

<source id="D13:2" doc="D13" title="billing_agent spend limits and approvals" section="billing_agent spend limits and approvals > Why the cap exists" date="2026-09-01" type="official">
## Why the cap exists

In March, a loop bug made `billing_agent` retry failed invoices without a step limit, and it used $2,900 of model calls in one night. The cap limits what any single bug can cost. It isn't a budget target: normal usage is about $2,200 a month.
</source>

<source id="D09:2" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Root cause" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Root cause

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed, and payments-gateway timed out instead of returning an error. `billing_agent` treated the timeouts as transient and retried each one until its step limit ran out.
</source>

Based on my analysis of incidents and documentation, here are the monitoring gaps that our incidents have exposed:

## 1. **No freshness/content accuracy monitoring** ([D10:2])

**Incident INC-2067** revealed that `research_agent` had perfect latency and zero errors because it was serving cached answers—but those answers were 4-7 days stale. Users only discovered the problem by manually comparing answers against source material.

*Gap*: Our monitoring collects latency, error rate, and session counts, but nothing measures whether agent responses are actually current and accurate relative to real-time knowledge changes.

---

## 2. **Poor visibility during infrastructure outages** ([D11:2], [D11:3])

**Incident INC-2093** showed multiple critical monitoring failures:

- **No lag alerts**: Nothing alerted when the standby database fell 38 minutes behind the primary before the outage began
- **Agent list went dark**: When the registry became unreachable during the 42-minute outage, dashboards showed *nothing* instead of maintaining the last known good agent list
- **Blind on-call response**: Without visible agent data, on-call engineers couldn't identify which agents were affected during the outage
- **Silent failures**: The `support_agent` failed silently rather than notifying users about registry unavailability

*Gaps*: 
- Missing alerts for standby staleness (fixed with new 60-second lag alert)
- No fallback mechanism showing last-known state during outages  
- No graceful degradation message for users when services fail

---

## 3. **Dependency chain monitoring not fully captured** ([D09:0], [D09:2])

**Incident INC-2041** (`billing_agent`) showed that when a dependent service (auth-service certificate expired → payments-gateway timeouts), the upstream agent's monitoring metrics appeared normal until cascading failures accumulated.

*Gap*: Agent-level monitoring doesn't easily expose transitive dependencies or external service health failures at higher levels in the incident response workflow.

---

The fixes implemented after these incidents include adding staleness alerts, implementing last-good-state caching, improving silent failure messaging, and addressing dependency visibility. But the fundamental gap—monitoring that proves content accuracy and freshness rather than just operational health—remains.

answers:
Based on my investigation of our incident history and related documentation, here are the monitoring gaps that our incidents have exposed:

## Registry/Database Failover Issues (INC-2093)
**Gap:** No alerting on replication lag between primary and standby databases
- During the registry outage, the standby fell **38 minutes behind** the primary before any alert fired
- The failover should have taken ~5 minutes but took 42 minutes because of this silent lag
- When registry became unavailable, monitoring dashboard went completely blank with no agent list visible
- *Documentation*: "For the whole outage, monitoring showed no agents at all, so the on-call engineer couldn't tell which agents were affected" [D11:2]

## Configuration Change Blind Spots (INC-2067)
**Gap:** No alerting or validation for production configuration changes that silently degrade service quality
- kb-search cache TTL was changed from 7 hours to 7 days, causing outdated results to persist
- This went unnoticed for **10,080 minutes (~7 days)**
- No review/approval process existed for caching settings exceeding normal thresholds
- *Documentation*: "Every search that had been cached returned the version of each article from when it was first cached, so answers drifted further out of date each day" [D10:1]

## Certificate Expiration Detection (INC-2041)
**Gap:** No early warning alerts for infrastructure certificate expirations
- auth-service intermediate certificate expired at 06:00 with no prior notice
- Cascaded failure: payments-gateway timed out instead of returning proper errors
- led to billing_agent retries exhausting their step limits
- *Documentation*: "An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed" [D09:2]

## Summary of Identified Gaps
| Gap | What was missing | Consequence |
|-----|------------------|-------------|
| Replication lag detection | No alert when standby falls significantly behind primary | 38-minute blind period during failover |
| Config change oversight | No audit/review for TTL/cache settings > threshold | 7-day outage with degraded data |
| Certificate expiration | No proactive notification before expiry | Failed authentication cascade |
| Agent visibility during registry downtime | Dashboard showed no agents | Lost context for incident response |

The company has implemented fixes for some of these (e.g., 30-day certificate expiration alerts, 60-second standby lag alert), but these gaps represent systematic issues with how operational state changes are monitored and detected.

other monitoring infrastructure are available and running correctly.

content.text:
Based on my investigation of our incident history and related documentation, here are the monitoring gaps that our incidents have exposed:

## Registry/Database Failover Issues (INC-2093)
**Gap:** No alerting on replication lag between primary and standby databases
- During the registry outage, the standby fell **38 minutes behind** the primary before any alert fired
- The failover should have taken ~5 minutes but took 42 minutes because of this silent lag
- When registry became unavailable, monitoring dashboard went completely blank with no agent list visible
- *Documentation*: "For the whole outage, monitoring showed no agents at all, so the on-call engineer couldn't tell which agents were affected" [D11:2]

## Configuration Change Blind Spots (INC-2067)
**Gap:** No alerting or validation for production configuration changes that silently degrade service quality
- kb-search cache TTL was changed from 7 hours to 7 days, causing outdated results to persist
- This went unnoticed for **10,080 minutes (~7 days)**
- No review/approval process existed for caching settings exceeding normal thresholds
- *Documentation*: "Every search that had been cached returned the version of each article from when it was first cached, so answers drifted further out of date each day" [D10:1]

## Certificate Expiration Detection (INC-2041)
**Gap:** No early warning alerts for infrastructure certificate expirations
- auth-service intermediate certificate expired at 06:00 with no prior notice
- Cascaded failure: payments-gateway timed out instead of returning proper errors
- led to billing_agent retries exhausting their step limits
- *Documentation*: "An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed" [D09:2]

## Summary of Identified Gaps
| Gap | What was missing | Consequence |
|-----|------------------|-------------|
| Replication lag detection | No alert when standby falls significantly behind primary | 38-minute blind period during failover |
| Config change oversight | No audit/review for TTL/cache settings > threshold | 7-day outage with degraded data |
| Certificate expiration | No proactive notification before expiry | Failed authentication cascade |
| Agent visibility during registry downtime | Dashboard showed no agents | Lost context for incident response |

The company has implemented fixes for some of these (e.g., 30-day certificate expiration alerts, 60-second standby lag alert), but these gaps represent systematic issues with how operational state changes are monitored and detected.

## What happened

`research_agent` finds its sources through kb-search. On 2026-06-15 a config change set the kb-search cache's time-to-live to 7 days instead of 7 hours. Every search that had been cached returned the version of each article from when it was first cached, so answers drifted further out of date each day.
</source>

<source id="D10:3" doc="D10" title="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results" section="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results > What we changed" date="2026-06-24" type="official">
## What we changed

- kb-search's cache settings are now reviewed like code, and a time-to-live above 24 hours needs the Search team's approval.
- Each kb-search result now carries the date the article was last updated, and `research_agent` includes it when it cites a source.
- Reports produced during the affected week were flagged to their readers.
</source>

Based on my investigation of our incident history and related documentation, here are the monitoring gaps that our incidents have exposed:

## Registry/Database Failover Issues (INC-2093)
**Gap:** No alerting on replication lag between primary and standby databases
- During the registry outage, the standby fell **38 minutes behind** the primary before any alert fired
- The failover should have taken ~5 minutes but took 42 minutes because of this silent lag
- When registry became unavailable, monitoring dashboard went completely blank with no agent list visible
- *Documentation*: "For the whole outage, monitoring showed no agents at all, so the on-call engineer couldn't tell which agents were affected" [D11:2]

## Configuration Change Blind Spots (INC-2067)
**Gap:** No alerting or validation for production configuration changes that silently degrade service quality
- kb-search cache TTL was changed from 7 hours to 7 days, causing outdated results to persist
- This went unnoticed for **10,080 minutes (~7 days)**
- No review/approval process existed for caching settings exceeding normal thresholds
- *Documentation*: "Every search that had been cached returned the version of each article from when it was first cached, so answers drifted further out of date each day" [D10:1]

## Certificate Expiration Detection (INC-2041)
**Gap:** No early warning alerts for infrastructure certificate expirations
- auth-service intermediate certificate expired at 06:00 with no prior notice
- Cascaded failure: payments-gateway timed out instead of returning proper errors
- led to billing_agent retries exhausting their step limits
- *Documentation*: "An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed" [D09:2]

## Summary of Identified Gaps
| Gap | What was missing | Consequence |
|-----|------------------|-------------|
| Replication lag detection | No alert when standby falls significantly behind primary | 38-minute blind period during failover |
| Config change oversight | No audit/review for TTL/cache settings > threshold | 7-day outage with degraded data |
| Certificate expiration | No proactive notification before expiry | Failed authentication cascade |
| Agent visibility during registry downtime | Dashboard showed no agents | Lost context for incident response |

The company has implemented fixes for some of these (e.g., 30-day certificate expiration alerts, 60-second standby lag alert), but these gaps represent systematic issues with how operational state changes are monitored and detected.

### Handling Query Conflicts

Row version cleanup isn't the only potential cause of conflicts with standby queries. All index-only scans (including those that run on standbys) must use an MVCC snapshot that “agrees” with the visibility map. Conflicts are therefore required whenever `VACUUM` sets a page as all-visible in the visibility map containing one or more rows *not* visible to all standby queries. So even running `VACUUM` against a table with no updated or deleted rows requiring cleanup might lead to conflicts.
</source>

### How to Use Agent Mode in Detail

Use the `--agent` flag to run Prometheus in the Agent mode. The rest of the flags are either for both server and Agent or only for a specific mode. You can see which flag is for which mode by checking the last sentence of a flag's help string. "Use with server mode only" means it's only for server mode. If you don't see any mention like this, it means the flag is shared.

The Agent mode accepts the same scrape configuration with the same discovery options and remote write options. It also exposes a web UI on port 9095 with disabled query capabilities but shows build info, configuration, targets, and service discovery information as in a normal Prometheus server.
</source>

<source id="D09:2" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Root cause" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Root cause

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed, and payments-gateway timed out instead of returning an error. `billing_agent` treated the timeouts as transient and retried each one until its step limit ran out.
</source>

<source id="D09:3" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > What we changed" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## What we changed

- auth-service now alerts 30 days before any certificate expires.
- payments-gateway now returns an error immediately when a certificate check fails, instead of hanging.
- `billing_agent` stops retrying after three timeouts from the same service in one session.
</source>

<source id="D09:1" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Timeline" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Timeline

- 06:02 — `AgentErrorRateHigh` fired for `billing_agent`. No page: it was outside paging hours.
- 08:00 — The on-call engineer saw the alert and found every failed session stuck on the same payments-gateway call.
- 08:40 — The Payments team found that payments-gateway couldn't open connections to auth-service.
- 08:55 — The Identity team renewed the certificate. `billing_agent` recovered within two minutes.
</source>

<source id="D09:0" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Summary" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Summary

On 2026-04-08, `billing_agent` failed to issue invoices for 2 hours 15 minutes. Every attempt ended in a timeout from payments-gateway. No customer was charged twice, but 1,140 invoices went out late.
</source>

<source id="D04:2" doc="D04" title="Agent platform architecture overview" section="Agent platform architecture overview > How requests flow" date="2026-02-14" type="official">
## How requests flow

When a request reaches registry-api, it first asks auth-service to validate the `X-Registry-Key` header, then reads or writes registry-db. If auth-service is slow, every registry request is slow; if registry-db is unavailable, registry-api can't answer at all.

Monitoring gets its list of agents from registry-api every 30 seconds, then collects metrics from each agent on the list.
</source>

The failover should have taken about 5 minutes. It took 42 because the standby had fallen 38 minutes behind the primary, and nothing alerted on that lag. ## Timeline

- 14:10 — The primary registry-db host failed a disk check and failover started.
- 14:11 — `RegistryUnreachable` fired and paged the on-call engineer. The overview dashboard went blank.
- 14:20 — `support_agent` sessions began failing on their first registry lookup. `triage_agent` kept running but couldn't hand tickets over, so 212 tickets queued.
- 14:52 — The standby finished catching up and registry-api recovered. The queued tickets were handed over by 15:05.

<source id="D11:0" doc="D11" title="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover" section="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover > Summary" date="2026-08-29" type="official">
## Summary

On 2026-08-27, registry-api was unavailable for 42 minutes while registry-db failed over to its standby. Agents that look things up in the registry couldn't finish their tasks, and monitoring lost sight of every agent for the same period.
</source>

<source id="D11:3" doc="D11" title="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover" section="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover > What we changed" date="2026-08-29" type="official">
## What we changed

- An alert now fires when the standby falls more than 60 seconds behind.
- Monitoring keeps its last good agent list when the registry is unreachable, instead of showing nothing.
- `support_agent` now tells users the registry is unavailable instead of failing silently.
</source>

<source id="D04:1" doc="D04" title="Agent platform architecture overview" section="Agent platform architecture overview > Core services" date="2026-02-14" type="official">
## Core services

- **registry-api** — the Registry API. Stores every agent's configuration. Owned by the Platform team.
- **registry-db** — the Postgres database behind registry-api, with a hot standby for failover. Owned by the Platform team.
- **auth-service** — validates registry keys and issues the internal certificates services use to talk to each other. Owned by the Identity team.
- **monitoring** — collects latency and error metrics for every agent and raises alerts. Owned by the Observability team.
- **kb-search** — search over the internal knowledge base, with a response cache in front of it. Owned by the Search team.
</source>

### Handling Query Conflicts

Row version cleanup isn't the only potential cause of conflicts with standby queries. All index-only scans (including those that run on standbys) must use an MVCC snapshot that “agrees” with the visibility map. Conflicts are therefore required whenever `VACUUM` sets a page as all-visible in the visibility map containing one or more rows *not* visible to all standby queries. So even running `VACUUM` against a table with no updated or deleted rows requiring cleanup might lead to conflicts.
</source>

## Root cause

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed, and payments-gateway timed out instead of returning an error. `billing_agent` treated the timeouts as transient and retried each one until its step limit ran out.

<source id="D09:3" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > What we changed" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## What we changed

- auth-service now alerts 30 days before any certificate expires.
- payments-gateway now returns an error immediately when a certificate check fails, instead of hanging.
- `billing_agent` stops retrying after three timeouts from the same service in one session.
</source>

<source id="D09:1" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Timeline" date="2026-04-10" type="official">

- 06:02 — `AgentErrorRateHigh` fired for `billing_agent`. No page: it was outside paging hours.
- 08:00 — The on-call engineer saw the alert and found every failed session stuck on the same payments-gateway call.
- 08:40 — The Payments team found that payments-gateway couldn't open connections to auth-service.
- 08:55 — The Identity team renewed the certificate. `billing_agent` recovered within two minutes.
</source>

## How requests flow

When a request reaches registry-api, it first asks auth-service to validate the `X-Registry-Key` header, then reads or writes registry-db. If auth-service is slow, every registry request is slow; if registry-db is unavailable, registry-api can't answer at all.

Monitoring gets its list of agents from registry-api every 30 seconds, then collects metrics from each agent on the list.

- **auth-service** — validates registry keys and issues the internal certificates services use to talk to each other. Owned by the Identity team.
- **monitoring** — collects latency and error metrics for every agent and raises alerts. Owned by the Observability team.

Based on the official Registry API reference [D01:8], the registry has a rate limit of **60 requests per minute per key**. 

Key details:
- Limits apply per key, not per agent
- Requests past the limit return HTTP 429 with error code `REG-1009`
- A `Retry-After` header provides the number of seconds to wait before retrying

This rate limit was lowered from 100 to 60 requests per minute in the registry v2.4 update on 2026-05-12 [D03:2]. This change was made because some internal dashboards were polling too frequently, which slowed down the registry for agents sharing keys.

<source id="D01:8" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Rate limits" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Rate limits

Each key may make 60 requests per minute. Requests past the limit get HTTP 429 with error `REG-1009` and a `Retry-After` header giving the number of seconds to wait. Limits apply per key, not per agent, so two processes sharing one key share one limit.
</source>

<source id="D03:2" doc="D03" title="Registry changelog" section="Registry changelog > v2.4 — 2026-05-12" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## v2.4 — 2026-05-12

- Lowered the rate limit from 100 to 60 requests per minute per key. Some internal dashboards were polling hard enough to slow the registry for agents.

## Root cause

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed, and payments-gateway timed out instead of returning an error. `billing_agent` treated the timeouts as transient and retried each one until its step limit ran out.

<source id="D09:0" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Summary" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Summary

On 2026-04-08, `billing_agent` failed to issue invoices for 2 hours 15 minutes. Every attempt ended in a timeout from payments-gateway. No customer was charged twice, but 1,140 invoices went out late.
</source>

<source id="D09:3" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > What we changed" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## What we changed

- auth-service now alerts 30 days before any certificate expires.
- payments-gateway now returns an error immediately when a certificate check fails, instead of hanging.
- `billing_agent` stops retrying after three timeouts from the same service in one session.
</source>

<source id="D09:1" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Timeline" date="2026-04-10" type="official">

- 08:40 — The Payments team found that payments-gateway couldn't open connections to auth-service.
- 08:55 — The Identity team renewed the certificate. `billing_agent` recovered within two minutes.
</source>

#### Planning for High Availability

If primary restarts while commits are waiting for acknowledgment, those waiting transactions will be marked fully committed once the primary database recovers. There is no way to be certain that all standbys have received all outstanding WAL data at time of the crash of the primary. Some transactions may not show as committed on the standby, even though they show as committed on the primary. The guarantee we offer is that the application will not receive explicit acknowledgment of the successful commit of a transaction until the WAL data is known to be safely received by all the synchronous standbys.
</source>

#### Basic Configuration

Setting `synchronous_commit` to `remote_write` will cause each commit to wait for confirmation that the standby has received the commit record and written it out to its own operating system, but not for the data to be flushed to disk on the standby. This setting provides a weaker guarantee of durability than `on` does: the standby could lose the data in the event of an operating system crash, though not a PostgreSQL crash. However, it's a useful setting in practice because it can decrease the response time for the transaction. Data loss could only occur if both the primary and the standby crash and the database of the primary gets corrupted at the same time.
</source>

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:59" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Log-Shipping Standby Servers > Synchronous Replication > Basic Configuration" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
#### Basic Configuration

Once streaming replication has been configured, configuring synchronous replication requires only one additional configuration step: section guc-synchronous-standby-names must be set to a non-empty value. `synchronous_commit` must also be set to `on`, but since this is the default value, typically no change is required. (See section runtime-config-wal-settings and section runtime-config-replication-primary.) This configuration will cause each commit to wait for confirmation that the standby has written the commit record to durable storage. `synchronous_commit` can be set by individual users, so it can be configured in the configuration file, for particular users or databases, or dynamically by applications, in order to control the durability guarantee on a per-t
</source>

Prometheus values reliability. You can always view what statistics are

level of a private security report. On the other hand, the absence of arbitrary
sanity limits in some part of the code base is generally not worth a report on
its own.

#### Planning for High Availability

If primary restarts while commits are waiting for acknowledgment, those waiting transactions will be marked fully committed once the primary database recovers. There is no way to be certain that all standbys have received all outstanding WAL data at time of the crash of the primary. Some transactions may not show as committed on the standby, even though they show as committed on the primary. The guarantee we offer is that the application will not receive explicit acknowledgment of the successful commit of a transaction until the WAL data is known to be safely received by all the synchronous standbys.
</source>

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:63" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Log-Shipping Standby Servers > Synchronous Replication > Basic Configuration" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
#### Basic Configuration

Setting `synchronous_commit` to `remote_write` will cause each commit to wait for confirmation that the standby has received the commit record and written it out to its own operating system, but not for the data to be flushed to disk on the standby. This setting provides a weaker guarantee of durability than `on` does: the standby could lose the data in the event of an operating system crash, though not a PostgreSQL crash. However, it's a useful setting in practice because it can decrease the response time for the transaction. Data loss could only occur if both the primary and the standby crash and the database of the primary gets corrupted at the same time.
</source>

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:59" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Log-Shipping Standby Servers > Synchronous Replication > Basic Configuration" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
#### Basic Configuration

Once streaming replication has been configured, configuring synchronous replication requires only one additional configuration step: section guc-synchronous-standby-names must be set to a non-empty value. `synchronous_commit` must also be set to `on`, but since this is the default value, typically no change is required. (See section runtime-config-wal-settings and section runtime-config-replication-primary.) This configuration will cause each commit to wait for confirmation that the standby has written the commit record to durable storage. `synchronous_commit` can be set by individual users, so it can be configured in the configuration file, for particular users or databases, or dynamically by applications, in order to control the durability guarantee on a per-t
</source>

## When does it not fit?

Prometheus values reliability. You can always view what statistics are
available about your system, even under failure conditions. If you need 100%
accuracy, such as for per-request billing, Prometheus is not a good choice, as
the collected data will likely not be detailed and complete enough. In such a
case, you would be best off using some other system to collect and analyze the
data for billing, and Prometheus for the rest of your monitoring.

level of a private security report. On the other hand, the absence of arbitrary
sanity limits in some part of the code base is generally not worth a report on
its own.

## `histogram_quantiles()`

**This function has to be enabled via the feature
flag
`--enable-feature=promql-experimental-functions`.**

`histogram_quantiles(v instant-vector, quantile_label string, φ_1 scalar, φ_2 scalar, ...)` calculates multiple (between 1 and 10) φ-quantiles (0 ≤
φ ≤ 1) from a classic
histogram or from
a native histogram. Quantile calculation works the same way as in `histogram_quantile()`.

<source id="D09:2" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Root cause" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Root cause

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed, and payments-gateway timed out instead of returning an error. `billing_agent` treated the timeouts as transient and retried each one until its step limit ran out.
</source>

<source id="D09:0" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Summary" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Summary

On 2026-04-08, `billing_agent` failed to issue invoices for 2 hours 15 minutes. Every attempt ended in a timeout from payments-gateway. No customer was charged twice, but 1,140 invoices went out late.
</source>

<source id="D09:3" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > What we changed" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## What we changed

- auth-service now alerts 30 days before any certificate expires.
- payments-gateway now returns an error immediately when a certificate check fails, instead of hanging.
- `billing_agent` stops retrying after three timeouts from the same service in one session.
</source>

<source id="D09:1" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Timeline" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Timeline

- 06:02 — `AgentErrorRateHigh` fired for `billing_agent`. No page: it was outside paging hours.
- 08:00 — The on-call engineer saw the alert and found every failed session stuck on the same payments-gateway call.
- 08:40 — The Payments team found that payments-gateway couldn't open connections to auth-service.
- 08:55 — The Identity team renewed the certificate. `billing_agent` recovered within two minutes.
</source>

## Step 1: Check the target is allowed

<source id="D01:7" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Tiers and models" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Tiers and models

Every agent has a tier, and each tier allows a fixed set of models:

| Tier | Allowed models |
|---|---|
| `standard` | `claude-haiku`, `claude-sonnet` |
| `priority` | `claude-haiku`, `claude-sonnet`, `claude-opus` |

Moving an agent to `claude-opus` therefore means moving it to the `priority` tier first, which needs approval from its owner's budget holder. `claude-legacy` is deprecated and can't be assigned to any agent; existing agents on it keep working until 2026-10-31.
</source>

<source id="D01:4" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Creating an agent" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Creating an agent

`POST /agents` creates an agent. It needs a `write` key. The body must include `agent_id`, `model`, `tier` and `owner`; `status` defaults to `active`.

```json
{"agent_id": "triage_agent", "model": "claude-haiku", "tier": "standard", "owner": "support-team"}
```

Agent ids must be unique: reusing one returns `REG-1006`. The model must be allowed on the agent's tier (see "Tiers and models"), or the request fails with `REG-1007`.
</source>

## `histogram_quantiles()`

**This function has to be enabled via the feature
flag
`--enable-feature=promql-experimental-functions`.**

`histogram_quantiles(v instant-vector, quantile_label string, φ_1 scalar, φ_2 scalar, ...)` calculates multiple (between 1 and 10) φ-quantiles (0 ≤
φ ≤ 1) from a classic
histogram or from
a native histogram. Quantile calculation works the same way as in `histogram_quantile()`.
The second argument (a string) specifies the label name that is used to identify different quantiles in the query result.
```
histogram_quantiles(sum(rate(foo[1m])), "quantile", 0.9, 0.99)
# => {quantile="0.9"} 123
     {quantile="0.99"} 128
```

<source id="prometheus-docs/guides/open_metrics_2_0_migration.md:41" doc="prometheus-docs/guides/open_metrics_2_0_migration.md" title="OpenMetrics 2.0 Migration Guide for Client Libraries" section="OpenMetrics 2.0 Migration Guide for Client Libraries > CompositeValues > Summary" date="2026-09-23" type="vendor">
### Summary

**Rule:** In OM 2.0, a Summary Sample must contain Count, Sum, and a set of quantiles. In OM 1.0 these were all may. Exposers that previously omitted count or sum must now include them.

OM 1.0:
```
# TYPE http_request_duration_seconds_summary summary
http_request_duration_seconds_summary{quantile="0.5"} 0.013
http_request_duration_seconds_summary{quantile="0.9"} 0.025
http_request_duration_seconds_summary{quantile="0.99"} 0.10
http_request_duration_seconds_summary_sum 172.5
http_request_duration_seconds_summary_count 1027
```

OM 2.0:
```
# TYPE http_request_duration_seconds_summary summary
http_request_duration_seconds_summary {count:1027,sum:172.5,quantile:[0.5:0.013,0.9:0.025,0.99:0.10]}
```

* targets are discovered via service discovery or static configuration
* multiple modes of graphing and dashboarding support

## `histogram_quantiles()`

**This function has to be enabled via the feature
flag
`--enable-feature=promql-experimental-functions`.**

`histogram_quantiles(v instant-vector, quantile_label string, φ_1 scalar, φ_2 scalar, ...)` calculates multiple (between 1 and 10) φ-quantiles (0 ≤
φ ≤ 1) from a classic
histogram or from
a native histogram. Quantile calculation works the same way as in `histogram_quantile()`.
The second argument (a string) specifies the label name that is used to identify different quantiles in the query result.
```
histogram_quantiles(sum(rate(foo[1m])), "quantile", 0.9, 0.99)
# => {quantile="0.9"} 123
     {quantile="0.99"} 128
```

## Overview

The Registry API stores the configuration of every agent the company runs: its name, the model it uses, its tier, its owner and its status. Agents and internal tools read it to find out how an agent is configured, and owners write to it to change that configuration. The current version is v2.6.

All endpoints live under one base URL:

```
https://registry.internal.example/v2
```

Requests and responses are JSON. Timestamps are ISO 8601 in UTC.
</source>

<source id="D01:7" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Tiers and models" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Tiers and models

Every agent has a tier, and each tier allows a fixed set of models:

| Tier | Allowed models |
|---|---|
| `standard` | `claude-haiku`, `claude-sonnet` |
| `priority` | `claude-haiku`, `claude-sonnet`, `claude-opus` |

Moving an agent to `claude-opus` therefore means moving it to the `priority` tier first, which needs approval from its owner's budget holder. `claude-legacy` is deprecated and can't be assigned to any agent; existing agents on it keep working until 2026-10-31.
</source>

Prometheus's main features are:

* time series collection happens via a pull model over HTTP
* pushing time series is supported via an intermediary gateway
* targets are discovered via service discovery or static configuration
* multiple modes of graphing and dashboarding support

<source id="D09:2" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Root cause" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Root cause

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed, and payments-gateway timed out instead of returning an error. `billing_agent` treated the timeouts as transient and retried each one until its step limit ran out.
</source>

<source id="D09:0" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Summary" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Summary

On 2026-04-08, `billing_agent` failed to issue invoices for 2 hours 15 minutes. Every attempt ended in a timeout from payments-gateway. No customer was charged twice, but 1,140 invoices went out late.
</source>

<source id="D09:3" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > What we changed" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## What we changed

- auth-service now alerts 30 days before any certificate expires.
- payments-gateway now returns an error immediately when a certificate check fails, instead of hanging.
- `billing_agent` stops retrying after three timeouts from the same service in one session.
</source>

<source id="D09:1" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Timeline" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Timeline

- 06:02 — `AgentErrorRateHigh` fired for `billing_agent`. No page: it was outside paging hours.
- 08:00 — The on-call engineer saw the alert and found every failed session stuck on the same payments-gateway call.
- 08:40 — The Payments team found that payments-gateway couldn't open connections to auth-service.
- 08:55 — The Identity team renewed the certificate. `billing_agent` recovered within two minutes.
</source>

The [Docker Swarm service discovery][swarmsd] contains 3 different roles: nodes, services,
and tasks.

The first role, **nodes**, represents the hosts that are part of the Swarm. It
can be used to automatically monitor the Docker daemons or the Node Exporters
who run on the Swarm hosts.

The second role, **tasks**, represents any individual container deployed in the
swarm. Each task gets its associated service labels. One service can be backed by
one or multiple tasks.

The third one, **services**, will discover the services deployed in the
swarm. It will discover the ports exposed by the services. Usually you will want
to use the tasks role instead of this one.

**This function has to be enabled via the feature

## Summary

On 2026-04-08, `billing_agent` failed to issue invoices for 2 hours 15 minutes. Every attempt ended in a timeout from payments-gateway. No customer was charged twice, but 1,140 invoices went out late.
</source>

<source id="D09:1" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Timeline" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Timeline

- 06:02 — `AgentErrorRateHigh` fired for `billing_agent`. No page: it was outside paging hours.
- 08:00 — The on-call engineer saw the alert and found every failed session stuck on the same payments-gateway call.
- 08:40 — The Payments team found that payments-gateway couldn't open connections to auth-service.
- 08:55 — The Identity team renewed the certificate. `billing_agent` recovered within two minutes.
</source>

<source id="D09:2" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Root cause" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Root cause

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed, and payments-gateway timed out instead of returning an error. `billing_agent` treated the timeouts as transient and retried each one until its step limit ran out.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-docs/guides/dockerswarm.md:1" doc="prometheus-docs/guides/dockerswarm.md" title="Docker Swarm" section="Docker Swarm > Docker Swarm service discovery architecture" date="2026-09-23" type="vendor">
## Docker Swarm service discovery architecture

The [Docker Swarm service discovery][swarmsd] contains 3 different roles: nodes, services,
and tasks.

The first role, **nodes**, represents the hosts that are part of the Swarm. It
can be used to automatically monitor the Docker daemons or the Node Exporters
who run on the Swarm hosts.

The second role, **tasks**, represents any individual container deployed in the
swarm. Each task gets its associated service labels. One service can be backed by
one or multiple tasks.

The third one, **services**, will discover the services deployed in the
swarm. It will discover the ports exposed by the services. Usually you will want
to use the tasks role instead of this one.

Prometheus will only discover tasks and service that expose ports.
</source>
